(p = picture/image of the folio.)
(f = folio number.
(5 lines per folio, recto and verso.

(p.1a) (f.1a) (re 32425, meditation on the nine planets, the eight [verses] on the nine planets, the speech, the eight mantras. (p. 3a), (p. 3b, l1.)
May there be auspiciousness!
Salutation to Vighneśvara, the Hero, who is clad in white garlands and garments, the divine son of Īśa, the Lord of the Gaṇas. (l. 2)
The diagram of the nine planets with Jupiter as the assistant;
the diagram of the nine planets with the Sun as the assistant.
In the center of the altar, upon the pericarp of a graceful lotus,
stands the Sun with his seven horses, his body possessing the luster of dawn, with seven reins and two arms;
he was born in the beautiful lineage of Kāśyapa, which possesses manifold virtues.
Born from the syllable *kāliṅga*, facing east, holding a lotus in his hand, seated upon a lotus throne,
with lotus-like hands, two arms, and the luster of a lotus, the Sun-god— who rides seven horses,
who is the teacher of the world, and who wears a crown— may that deity grant us prosperity.
The Sun is red-colored; Soma is in the south-eastern quarter; the autumn months are ten; [the sage] born of Atri is from the region of the Yamunā.
(…) Upon that square pedestal, the Lord Gadādhara (Viṣṇu) is seated with his mother.

(l. 2. Clad in white garments and adorned with white ornaments, having two arms holding a second white staff, may the Moon-god—the essence of nectar, the bestower of boons—grant me prosperity; [may he grant] the white Moon. (l. 3. (…)
Mars is in the south, bearing a mace and a spear; facing the south, he is red and the bestower of boons from his trident.
Mars belongs to the region of Avanti and its trine; he is born in that family of Bhāradvāja.

May Aṅgāraka—born of fire, clad in red garments, with a red body, wearing a crown, four-armed, mounted upon a ram, bearing a mace, and holding a spear—be ever my peaceful granter of boons. [Now] Budha: The wise one, born of the Moon, dark-complexioned, three-eyed, seated upon a deer, four-armed, adorned with a crown, holding a rosary and a water-pot, and possessing a tranquil countenance, may he always grant me prosperity. [Now] Bṛhaspati: The preceptor of the gods, seated upon a swan, golden-hued, four-faced, four-armed, wearing a crown, and holding a rosary, a water-pot, a staff, and a book, may he always grant me wisdom. [Now] Śukra: The son of Bhṛgu, seated upon a bull, white-complexioned, four-armed, wearing a crown, and holding a rosary, a water-pot, a staff, and a book, may he always grant me eloquence. [Now] Śani: The son of the Sun, seated upon a donkey, black-complexioned, three-eyed, four-armed, wearing a crown, and holding a rosary, a water-pot, a staff, and a book, may he always grant me long life. [Now] Rāhu: The son of Siṃhikā, seated upon a camel, smoke-colored, four-armed, wearing a crown, and holding a sword, a shield, a rosary, and a water-pot, may he always grant me freedom from fear. [Now] Ketu: Born of smoke, clothed in red garments, with a red body, wearing a crown, four-armed, mounted upon a goat, bearing a mace, and holding a spear, may he always be my peaceful granter of boons. Aṅgāraka. [Now] Budha.
Facing upward, born of Mākhada, situated on a lion, belonging to the Ātreya lineage, and standing within a circle of arrows;
he who knows the bearer of the club upon his broad thighs; in the region of the northeast... wearing yellow garments, with a yellow body;
wearing a crown, possessing yellow luster, holding a staff, two-armed, and bearing the moon-sword, he is the son of Soma.
Tranquil, the wise one (*budha*) is a bestower of boons;

he is seated upon a long, four-cornered throne in the north, facing the north, with a gentle countenance and a radiant luster. He is the preceptor (*guru*). On the chariot (*radha*), the Earth-goddess stands, her face turned toward the north.
Holding a staff, a rosary, and a water-vessel, the one known as Siddha, the giver of boons, lives long in the land of Sindh.

Wearing golden garments, with a golden body, crowned, four-armed, the teacher of the gods, and tranquil—he who holds a staff, a water-pot, and likewise a rosary—may he grant me his boon. [Salutation] to Bṛhaspati.
In the east is Śukra; born from the jar of Bhṛgu, he is Bhārgava, facing eastward.
He is mounted upon a chariot in the five corners, holding a staff, a rosary, the gesture of granting boons, and a water-vessel.

Clad in white robes, with a white body, wearing a crown, four-armed, and tranquil—the preceptor of the Daityas—holds a staff and a water-pot; may the dull-witted ones [of] the fault of nakedness be for my [protection]. Śukra. Śani.

Cāpāsana is blue in color, facing west; he belongs to the Kāśyapa lineage and is highly praised as a bestower of boons while holding a trident and a bow in the western direction. He is born in the region of Saurāṣṭra and is the son of the Sun.
Wearing blue garments and having a blue body, he wears a crown and stands upon a vulture, striking terror with his bow.

May the four-armed son of the Sun, who is peaceful and slow-moving, grant me boons. Śani, Rāhu, Paiṭhīnasa, born in the country of Barbaras, seated on a winnowing basket, [mounted on] a lion, and smoke-colored— may they likewise grant me boons.

Facing south, in the region of Nirṛti, may Rāhu— the bestower of boons, with dark-complexioned skin, holding a sword and a shield, clad in black garments, possessing a dark body, wearing a crown, with a formidable face, bearing a scimitar and a trident, four-armed, and mounted upon a divine tiger— grant me his favor. (To Rāhu.)
Ketu,
whose seat is a banner, born of the Jaimini lineage, stands in the middle of the altar with a most variegated complexion;
facing south, he holds a sword in the direction of the wind and possesses eight hundred comets.
Smoky-colored, with two arms, bestowing boons, bearing a mace, seated upon a vulture, with a deformed face,
and his body adorned with a crown and armlets— may that peaceful Gaṇa be my banner.
Wearing divine garments, may Durgā Bhadrakālī, the bestower of happiness, [be my banner].
One should always meditate upon Kātyāyanī, the destroyer of death and the bestower of all boons.
(2) Salutation to the Lord of Obstacles, the Hero, who is adorned with white garlands and garments, the divine son of Īśa, the Master of the Gaṇas. (3)
Salutations again and again to Kṣetrapālavajra, the remover of all defects, the bestower of victory upon the world, and the creator of creation;
salutations to Indra, the granter of fearlessness and the one who directly bestows gentleness.
Salutations again and again to the destroyer of evil, the slayer of all enemies, the bestower of well-being.
(5) O Vāstoṣpati, salutations to you, the pacifier of all defects, the warder-off of all sins, and the eternal giver of fortune. (6)
Salutations to Śiva, together with Ambā, his attendants, and his son;

salutations again and again to him who is with Nandin, with Gaṅgā, and with the Bull. Salutations to the Conqueror of Death; salutations to Acyuta; salutations to the Bestower of Fearlessness; salutations to the Sacrificial Priest; salutations to Vāstupuruṣa.
Just as Mount Mahāmeru is for all the gods,
so too is the Vāstupuruṣa in my house for the gods beginning with Brahmā.
Salutations to you, O Lord who dwells within the earth!
Grant prosperity, wealth, grain, and other blessings in my home. [Blank] ...
Āditya, Candra, Bhauma, Budha, Guru, Bhṛguja, Bhānuja, Rāhu, and Ketu.
Having bowed down perpetually at the three junctions of the day to those who are the causes for the stability and prosperity of the world’s emergence—

these horses of the Sun in the circle of light, together with the hosts of stars and the zodiac signs beginning with Aries— I, assuming a form of power, pray with devotion to these best of gods who move through the sky.

At the time of dawn, those who have performed meritorious deeds obtain from the tips of the hands of young women that ancient food, accompanied by *jambīra* fruit, filled with oil, and mixed with *kāravallī* leaves and mango juice.
Reclining upon the waters, the sole heart’s delight of the world, especially manifesting his form at dawn—
the ancient bestower of health to all men, whom the performers of merit attain. May there be auspiciousness.
One should meditate upon Viṣṇu, who wears white garments, who is moon-colored, four-armed, and has a serene countenance, for the pacification of all obstacles.
May there be auspiciousness. [The *Vighneśvarāṣṭaka*].

For the pacification of all obstacles, one should meditate upon Viṣṇu, who wears white garments, who is moon-colored, four-armed, and has a gracious countenance. At the commencement of all undertakings, Vāgīśa and the other deities, being well-disposed, [grant success].
I bow to that elephant-faced one, by whose salutation all have accomplished their purpose.
Salutations to you, O Gaṇapati, who are worshipped by Vighneśa, Brahmā, the Sun, the Moon, Indra, and Upendra; salutations to the Brāhmaṇas, O Lord of Brahman!

Saffron-colored, endowed with four arms, having the face of an elephant and a crown with a jeweled casket; holding a goad, a sweetmeat, a tusk, and a noose; with eyes like fire, possessing the form of Gaṇanātha;
with an elephantine face that roars in battle, O Śarvarī, you are the leader of this [assembly].
He whose eyes are as pure as lotuses, the foremost son of Kālakaṇṭha.
One should meditate upon the Lord Vighnarāja, who is worshipped by the immortals and gods, who is rich in [the removal of] obstacles, and who is the protector even from Yama;
he is the destroyer of sins through his presence and has shattered the [false] discernment of the wicked. (L6)
I worship the Lord of Obstacles, the sun to the darkness of impediments;
the Lord of the hosts of gods and asuras, with beautiful hair,
the seer among seers, the Lord of Ganas, equal to the sacrifice.
O Bhava, O Gaṇapati, whose body is like a lotus!
Victory, victory to you, O Gaṇapati; divine salutations to you!
You whose feet rest upon the broad slopes of the mountains of the gods on earth, and who are exalted by the streams of ichor flowing from the temples of your elephant head.
I take refuge in the formidable Vināyaka, who has blossoming claws, whose ornament is a lotus, the son of Śiva, the Lord of the Gaṇas, the bestower of fearlessness,
the giver of desired fruits to his devotees, consecrated for the destruction of all obstacles,
radiant with golden earrings, and possessed of large tusks.
May it be auspicious!

Having established [the time] in the four directions, [it is determined by] the ninth, the seventh of Māgha, and the ninth, eighth, and seventh nāḍīs; if [the time] is deficient, one should perform [the rite] earlier.

O dear one, a wise man should cause those who are uninitiated, those with hair on their heads, the fallen, and those with physical defects to perform the ritual bathing after first having them seen and touched.
And during a festival in that village, if a human being dies or is born, O Śiva, upon the occurrence of such a defilement of the village, one should quickly abandon it; then,
having performed the purification rite consisting of sweeping and the sprinkling of water and so forth, [the area becomes pure].
Having recited the Aghora mantra one hundred times, one should perform the pacifying oblation (*śāntihoma*).

Even if he has been initiated, if he is an only son and his mother or father should die, he should perform only the funeral consecration (*saṃskāra*); at the conclusion of the sacrifice, there shall be the period of impurity (*sūtaka*).

The author of all the Sūtras declares that there is no fault [in eating] during a festival for a deity, at the consecration of an image, during a religious vow, at the initiation ceremony, or at the time of the consecratory bath.
Beginning from the eleventh day up to the sixteenth,
and likewise the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* on the seventeenth day.
A spear, an arrow, a sword, an umbrella, a noose, and likewise the gesture of fearlessness;
a thunderbolt, a bow, a shield, a cock, a goad, and the gesture of granting boons.
And he was mounted upon a peacock, endowed with all auspicious marks.
Born from that, there is the [goddess] Līlā on the left and the right;
she is endowed with all ornaments and adorned with every kind of finery.
The god who grants victory with all weapons has six faces; his form is the bow together with the quiver. At the time of dawn, one should perform the worship of Śiva.
O Goddess, that which is obtained in a thousand years is attained in a single day.
When the transit occurs in Capricorn, everyone is afflicted by the power [of the affliction].
One should worship the gods, beginning with the Sun, for one who has been released from that affliction;
and on the following day, one should release a bull among men.
At that time, there were also processions for the deities, as well as for the *āghrā* and others;
likewise, having touched the flowers above the lamps and having gazed upon them, there was the ritual sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*).
The wise one should perform the placement of the five Brahmās, the binding of the directions, and the veiling; then,
having displayed the trident mudrā and joined his palms at the heart with the mantra ending in *namaḥ*,
the preceptor should utter the *culīka* mantra while taking up the lamp.
For the purpose of removing defects of the channels, one should cast a lamp upon the eyes,
and likewise upon the mouth, the eyes, the tip of the nose, the throat, the chest, and the feet.
Having extracted each [syllable] ending with the left foot in the form of the *praṇava* (Oṃ),
these constitute the characteristics of the lamp.
The first is in the right eye, the second in the left eye, and the third above the forehead; now hear how it is with the fourth.
One should encircle [the deity] from the crown of the head down to the feet, ending at the body;
the first [encirclement] is for the protection of the earth, and the second is for the intermediate space.
The third [circumambulation] is for the protection of heaven, consisting of the worship of the lamp and the circumambulation;
the vessel, moreover, should be the form of Śakti, while the fire is the form of Śiva.

One should prepare the lamp in this manner: the flame of the best [lamp] is one finger-breadth (*yuga-aṅgula*), that of the middling is three finger-breadths, and that of the inferior is two finger-breadths.
(Ālayapradakṣiṇam – The Fruit of the Oblation, side heading)

Upon seeing sexual intercourse during a festival, while walking on a street, at a decorated gate, in a temple of Śiva, or at the time of death, one should perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma).
First, having circumambulated the temple, [one should go to] the second village;
then, having circumambulated the temple again, one follows the sequence of the rite of circumambulation.

Incense, lamps, food offerings, the water-pot, and the *ārātri* lamp should be presented during festivals, during the performance of rites, at the decorated gateway, and within the temple of Śiva. Upon seeing sexual intercourse or a death, one should perform a propitiatory fire-offering (*śāntihoma*).
Whoever performs [a rite] dedicated to Śiva, having first designated it for the removal of sin (aghapūrva), [attains the fruit].
One should not observe impurity regarding that substance which is fit for a deity;
whatever substance is dedicated to Śiva, that substance is called Śiva.
Just as a substance becomes worthy of the Dharma when it possesses the Dharma,
so too a substance that has not been offered to Śiva is proclaimed to be impure.
The surrounding area bestows fruit, and for one seeking knowledge, it bestows accomplishment.

[He should offer] the oblation that bestows the fruit of liberation and the accomplishment of desired goals. Then, having strewn [the ground] with *darbha* grass, he should prepare the sacrificial ladle (*sruk*) and spoon (*sruva*), which bestow the fruit of prosperity and the nourishment of clarified butter (*ājya*).
The vessel that grants the seeker of recitation what he desires is the remover of sin for the two who offer the fuel-sticks.

One should offer the *caru* oblation which bestows divinity and peace, and destroys disturbances within the kingdom. One should offer parched grain (*lāja*) for the sake of enjoyment, sovereignty, prosperity, happiness, fame, and auspiciousness.
One should offer rice (*dhānya*) which grants sons, enjoyment, the attainment of daughters, victory, and the status of a lord of wealth; it bestows success.

Milk bestows the fruit of happiness; curd, honey, and beauty grant splendor; flour-based preparations such as cakes and molasses-fruit provide enjoyment; and betel-leaf brings about the destruction of evil.

Incense bestows the fruits of glory, fame, and enjoyment; it grants the accomplishment of all aims and liberates one from evil. At every step, with flames and ashes and so forth, the fire grants all fruits and the state of Śiva. The final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) grants union (*sāyujya*). The sixteen-fold service, the fruit, the music, and the auspiciousness [are likewise attained].
Incense removes sins; a lamp is the destroyer of death.
There is no fear from any lamp; therefore, one should cause a lamp to be made at all times.
The bull-lamp, the horse-sacrifice, and the human-sacrifice grant the attainment of sons;
the jar-lamp brings great peace, and the collyrium-rite yields great fruit.
The asterism *Sarvasiddhi* brings success; the *Rathadīpa* brings subjugation (*vaśya*).
Ash is for the protection of the three worlds, and the mirror increases the world.
The parasol bestows sovereignty, and the fly-whisk bestows good fortune.
The fan, which brings all auspiciousness, and the cluster of palm leaves, which bestows happiness.

The complete study of the Vedas leads to liberation; the chanting of the Rudra-hymns bestows auspiciousness (*śiva*); the water for washing the feet destroys sin, while the water for sipping brings about prosperity.
The *arghya* [offering] brings success to one's actions; these [elements] purify the fruits [of karma]. The *mardala* drum brings happiness, and the *tāla* [rhythm] shall be the remover of sorrow.
The *paṭaha* drum removes evil; the *bherī* drum increases one's progeny;
the *priya* in the left hand brings what is dear; and the *gāndhāra* brings happiness.
The *jhallarī* brings desired objects, while the *kumbhavādya* bestows liberation.
The instrumental music of the *nāḍī-sandhāna* yields the fruit of ten million sacrifices;
likewise, the flute and vocal song increase one's sons and grandsons.
The joining of speech to the drum-skin brings victory through the sound of musical instruments;
when accompanied by the blast of the conch, it wards off all diseases.
Likewise, dance, instrumental music, and song increase one's lifespan.
Dancing leads to the increase of meditative concentration; likewise, pure dance is auspicious.
[The Fivefold Activity of Somāskanda]
The collection of earth for the site, the planting of the seed-sprouts,
the consecration of the bull, and the consecration of the base of the banner and the weapons.
Thus there shall be the beating of the drum and likewise the invocation at the twilight rites;
the hoisting of the banner has been described, as well as the worship of the sacrificial pavilion.

The auspicious rite of binding the protective thread (*rakṣābandhana*) is declared to be the act of creation (*sṛṣṭikarma*); likewise, the procedure for the fire-ritual (*agnikāryavidhi*), as well as the circumambulation with offerings (*balibhramaṇa*). On the sixth day, the procession (*yātrā*) takes place; thus is the stability (*sthiti*) described here.
Thus was the mounting of the chariot, accompanied by the expedition for the hunt.
The worship of Kṛṣṇagandhā and the withdrawal are also described;
likewise, the dismissal, the sprout, the sacrifice to Caṇḍa, and concealment.
Favor, the procession of power, the festival of the fivefold rites (*pañcakṛtya*),
as well as the auspicious rite of sowing seeds (*aṅkurārpaṇa*), the hoisting of the banner,
and the binding of the protective thread— these are declared to be the ritual acts of emanation (*sṛṣṭikarma*).
The rite of installation is proclaimed as being joined with the festival of the vehicle, likewise with the performance of fire-offerings, and accompanied by the procession of the ritual oblations.

Combined with the powder of *rajani*, as well as mounting the chariot (*rathārohaṇa*), one should perform the festival of the black-bodied one (*kālāṅgarotsava*); this is proclaimed as the "Withdrawal" (*saṃhāra*).
The festival of silence, the state of concealment, the journey toward liberation, and grace—
all these are served by the devotees through the path of devotion.
The creation, the wonder of maintenance, and the bond;
the non-heavy dissolution and the application of camphor ointment;
the favor, the Lord of the Palanquin, and the witnessing of the dance at dawn.
The Fivefold Activity of Naṭeśvara.
The form of Naṭeśvara is [the letter] *na* (–);
the ḍamaru is the form of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), while withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) is the form of fire;
maintenance (*sthiti*) is the face of the serpent, while concealment (*tirobhāva*) is the contracted [form].
Fearlessness and grace, whose very nature consists of the fivefold activity;
when the sun has risen to the brilliance of Rudra at the time of dawn, and the bow [the sign of Sagittarius] is the ascendant;
on a festival day, whether joined with or separated from the play of the gods, as taught in the scriptures concerning creation and so forth.
[The Activity of the Destruction of Naṭeśvara]

Worship, the emanation of the food offering (*naivedya*), maintenance, the illustrious *balināyaka*, incense, lamp, the *bali* offering, the fire sacrifice (*homa*), and withdrawal— these are thus described. [One should perform] the concealment of the palanquin and so forth, as well as the favor of the *kṣetrapāla*.
Thus dancing, these five [deities] embody the nature of the fivefold activities;
they are seated comfortably together with Umā,
auspiciously beautiful, and indeed have the moon as their crest-ornament.
Gaṅgādhara—these five are proclaimed as the form of emanation (*sṛṣṭirūpa*);
likewise Bhikṣāṭana, Kaṅkāla, and Vīrabhadra.
The standing form is proclaimed as having one foot mounted upon a bull (the activity of Naṭeśvara and Saṃhāra).
[Then there are] Gaja, Tripuraghna, Manmatha (the destroyer of the established order),
Kālasaṃhāraṇa, and Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
Thus, he is described as having five forms and as the one who performs the withdrawal;
[he is] Kirāta, the form of dance, and the destroyer of the poison of the half-body of Hari and Hara.
These five are proclaimed as the manifestations of the Liṅgodbhava [Liṅga]:
Cakraprasāda-vighna, Caṇḍeśānugraha, Somāskanda, and likewise Ardhanārī.
Thus, this fivefold form is known as Anugraha;
having firmly anointed all the limbs with fragrant aloe-wood pastes.
Having draped a new cloth over Droṇa, who is adorned with garlands,
and having paraded him through the four streets, he stands before the city gate.
Should there be a defect in the vision [of the image], or if a doubt arises regarding the touch of Śaṅkara;
That which exists within the interval, free from both touch and non-touch, is the Lord.
Thus, the wise one should cause the ceremonial bathing to be performed outside, within the gateway;
[this concludes the thirty-two marks].
"Endowed with the thirty-two marks" means as follows:
five long, four in four [parts], five subtle, six elevated,
seven red, three deep, and two broad, as it is said.
The two [joints] between the arms and the eyes, the knees, the nose, and the space between the breasts.
The five long [parts] have been enumerated as the neck, the shank, the middle of the back, and the two [shoulders];
these four have not been mentioned by the wise in the *Hṛtsva*.
The finger-joints are subtle; the hair is like that of the Arka plant;
the nails, the two armpits, the belly, the chest, the bridge of the nose, and the forehead [are likewise].
And those who belong to all the assemblies say that there are six such elevations:
the palms of the hands, the soles of the feet, the eyes, and the nails.
Furthermore, the palate, the tongue, and the lips are proclaimed as the seven [smooth] surfaces.
The state of being the essence of sound (svarasvatva), the navel, and the three directions are proclaimed as the "three-fold bearer" (tridigbhara).
The chest and the forehead are praised when they are two [units] in width;
thus have the thirty-two marks been proclaimed, as they were seen by the Lion of Men.
[The Amulet]

Having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) in front of the deity, having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be made, and having sprinkled [the area] with water; then, upon the mound: *oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to the Support-Energy (*ādhāraśakti*). Having worshipped the three principles (*tattva*) on the tripod, and having honored the sixfold arising seat (*ṣaḍutthāsana*) in the vessels; over the rice grains: *oṃ hāṃ*, *huṃ phaṭ* to the Weapon, salutation. On the support for the ashes: *oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to the Principle of Māyā (*māyātattva*). In the ashes: *oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to Lakulīśvara. On the protective thread (*pratisarasūtra*): *oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to Ananta.

Regarding the betel: having worshipped Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra; and having worshipped the coconut fruit with "Oṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to Vighneśvara," and having offered incense and lamps to these, and presented the food offering; then, taking the protective thread (*pratisara-sūtra*), one should bind it on the portion of Rudra with the *Īśāna* mantra. Having placed it in the right hand of the [male] images and in the left hand of the female deities (*śakti*s), and having offered the sacred ash (*bhasman*), one should dismiss them all.
This is the procedure for the flowers (*puṣpavidhi*).
One should worship Śiva with one’s own self, or even with festive offerings and flowers—
such as jasmine, blue lotuses, red lotuses, jasmine, *pannaga*, and *campaka*.
And with aśoka, śveta-mandāra, karṇikāra, and ambaka; and with karavīra, arka, mandāra, śamī, nagara, and kesara.
With *kuśa*, *apāmārga*, and *kadamba* flowers born from *droṇa* trees,
as well as white and golden *dhurdhūra* and red *kāñcana*—
these blossoms of the *palāśa* and *pāṭalī* are recorded as being highly praised.
One should repeatedly wash the head of the deity after placing upon it bilva, tulasī, dhūrdhūra, kalhāra, and hemapuṣpaka flowers.
Tulasī [should be offered] at the end of a year, and likewise bilva every six months.

The lotus [is used] for twelve months; other flowers are for a single day. The bilva, apāmārga, mango, damana, maru, arjuna, nandyāvarta, śamyā, and mallikā growing on the stalks [are likewise prescribed].
With *saugandhika*, *asanā*, *gastī*, *sinduvāra*, *śephālikā*, and *arjuna*;
with *dūrvā*, *tālaśikhāṅka*, *logabharī*, *surabhikā*, and *śamī*;
with *muṇḍikā*, *radamana*, *bhṛṅgāra*, and *paribhaṇḍraka*.
Jambu and kuśāgra—these are the recommended collections of leaves.
If the previously mentioned flowers are unavailable, one should worship Śiva with these leaves;
and if even the leaves are unavailable, one should worship him with fruits as well.
With *bījāpūra* fruits, *jambīra* citrons, auspicious plantains, and pomegranates—
one should worship Śiva with these fruits that provide immediate satisfaction.
Having washed the liṅga again and again, one should worship it at the three junctions of the day with tulasī leaves, bilva leaves, golden flowers, and pearls.
On Sunday, it should be bilva; on Monday, tulasī;
on Tuesday, kapittha; and likewise on Wednesday, māduliṅga.
Bṛhaspati, Dāñcava, Bhārgava,
Jambu, Śani, and Viṣṇukrānti— these are said here to be the *vāra* flowers. With those respective flowers, whether grown in water or on land, one should worship Śiva.

Having worshipped and sprinkled [the deity] with those [flowers] out of devotion, one is glorified in the world of Śiva. He who, having personally gathered flowers, worships Śiva correctly, and who constantly worships Śiva with devotion— [Śiva] himself directly accepts those [offerings].
Flowers from the finest garden are the best; those grown newly are middling; those from a marketplace and those obtained by begging are the lowest, and they shall be fruitless.
The *karavīra* flower is superior to a thousand *arka* flowers;
the deity is situated within it in the form of a *liṅga* and pedestal (*pīṭha*). That flower and the golden flower [yield] a *yuga* for every year of worship.

"It shall not become his discarded offering"— this is the certain conclusion of the scripture. By worshipping Nīlakaṇṭha with even a single *karavīra* flower, whether white or scented, one shall deliver ten million members of one's lineage.
The *bilva* leaf is superior to a thousand *karavīra* flowers;
the wise know that the three *bilva* leaves represent the powers of will, knowledge, and action.
By the sight, touch, or even the salutation of a bilva leaf, the sin committed during a day and night is destroyed; there is no doubt about this.
O Nārada, even with dry or withered bilva leaves, [the same result is attained].
One who worships the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain is liberated from all sins.
(L4) One should worship the true liṅga with bilva leaves and fruits;
being completely freed from all sins, one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
One should avoid insects and the like, as well as theft and spider-silk;
[one should also avoid] the leaf called *kunda*, the leaf of a parrot, the *bilva* fruit, and the *nirguṇḍī*.
Having offered five *kapittha* leaves and five *bilva* leaves,
and having worshipped Śiva with the mantras of the nature of space (*vyomātman*),
a single lotus leaf is superior to a thousand *bilva* leaves.
The *bakapuṣpa* flower excels over a thousand lotus petals;
a thousand *bakapuṣpa* flowers are surpassed by one *dhurdhūraka*;
and a thousand *dhurdhūraka* flowers are surpassed by the *bṛhatpuṣpa*.
The *droṇa* flower is superior to a thousand *bṛhatpuṣpa* flowers;
the *apāmārga* flower is superior to a thousand *droṇa* flowers.
A single *kuśa* flower is superior to a thousand *apāmārga* plants;
a glorious blue lotus is better than a thousand *kuśa* flowers.
Among all species of flowers, the blue lotus is the most excellent;
there shall be no flower equal to the blue lotus that can be called a "blue flower."
A single act of devotion excels thousands of blue lotuses;
likewise, white, red, and blue [lotuses] correspond to those [qualities], such as the *sāttvika* and the others.
One should designate yellow-colored flowers as the "mixed" (miśraka) type;
with the exception of the blue lotus, one should avoid all others that belong to the quality of darkness (tāmasa).
The *nandyāvarta*, the *śriyāvarta*, and the white *arka* flower are beneficial at sunrise; likewise, the *karavīra* flower and the *droṇī* plant are beneficial at midday on the mountain.
One should offer Mallikā at dusk; Kṛṣṇadhurdhūra and Campaka are beneficial at evening;
and Kadamba, Kanakā, Jāti, and Dvikarṇa at midnight.
The *droṇa*, the white lotus (*śvetapadma*), the *jātī*, the *bahuparṇikā*, the *nandyāvarta*, the *śriyāvarta*, the *mandāra*, the *śatapatrikā*, the white *arkā*,
the *mālatī*, the *bilva*, the *pannaga*, and likewise the *kurava*.
One should designate flowers such as these as *sāttvika*.
Likewise, the red lotus (*raktotpala*), the lotus (*padma*), the *dhurdhūra*, the two types of *bṛhatī*,
the *palāśa*, the *pāṭala*, and so forth, one should designate as *rājasa*.
In the Kālottara (p. 23b, f. 10, l.
1): Karaja, vakula, kāśa, śirīṣa, and likewise ketakī;
lāṅgalī, pomegranate, cāpa, śrīparṇī, and vibhītaka.
One should avoid the Bandhūka, Kunda, and Āyudha flowers, as well as cotton, Nimbakaṇṭhaka, Kiṃśuka, Jamantī, and Kumuda lotuses.
One should avoid flowers that are unripe, over-ripe, or still in bud;
those infested by hair or insects; those covered by spiderwebs;
and even those that have fallen of their own accord, even if they are gathered in a cloth.
One should discard flowers that have been kept for even a single day and those that are damaged.
One should not worship Viṣṇu with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), nor Vināyaka with *tulasy* leaves, nor Maheśāna with *dūrvā* grass; furthermore, one should not offer *naraka* grass to Maheśvara.
One should avoid flowers that are scentless, lacking fragrance, or foul-smelling;
[this is stated] in the *Suprabheda*.
During festivals and the like, on processions, at meals, and during ritual acts.
In the *Kālottara*, it is stated that while all [ornaments] are to be avoided, they are always to be accepted as ornaments;
likewise, black-limbed flowers, the *mahiṣākṣī* flower, and the *puṣpikā* flower [are to be used].
The goddess Umā should worship with flowers from the Śiṃśumāra tree;
one should not offer a flower produced from the garden of the king of gods to the household deity.
Whoever worships the *arka-liṅga* with fragrant *yamuka* flowers and with garlands woven from various [materials],
shall obtain infinite fruit.
A man should worship the *liṅga* after encircling the pedestal (*vedi*) with garlands.
Śiva, together with the Goddess and his son, is delighted by this worshipful practice. O Goddess, the altar of the *liṅga* is the *liṅga* itself; Maheśvara is manifest therein.
By the worship of those two, both the Goddess and the God are worshipped.

Adorned from the pedestal upward with hanging flower garlands and the like,
surrounded by all the most wonderful Great Vehicles graced with divine flowers, that glorious one shall go happily to the city of Śiva.
If she, the destroyer of Rākṣasas, is worshipped with leaves, she shall grant all accomplishments;
if she is worshipped with flowers, she likewise becomes the bestower of all siddhis.

Having first worshipped the limbs of dissolution (*layāṅga*) with the mantras of Śiva and Brahmā, and having prostrated and received the command of the Lord, one should then worship the limbs of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga*). (Somaśambhu, verse 3)
In the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"Worship is the means for attaining the state of Śiva's perfect qualities and for the enjoyment [of those qualities];
it is the reintegration of the limbs [of the self] and the union of the self with Śiva."
One should worship Īśāna on the eastern petal, Nara on the eastern petal,
Aghora on the southern petal, and likewise Vāmadeva on the northern petal.
The unarisen [lotus] is on the western petal; the heart is on the fire-petal.
It is said to be one *aṅgula* in width, which is half of the [total] width.
It may be made of gold, silver, or other [precious materials].
Half of that should be known as the middling, and half of that again becomes the smallest.
In the *Kāmika*:
"The pure practitioner, having taken up a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or even two pieces of bell-metal, or he may make it of pure bronze."
In the subtle [practice],
having smeared with cow dung, one should place a mandala before the deity;
having washed the vessel, one should fill it with the food offering (naivedya).
In the middle [section], there is milk and curd, covered with seasonings, salts, and side-dishes, and combined with fruits and molasses.
It should be provided with clarified butter and ghee, covered with a cloth, and accompanied by soups,
cakes, side dishes, and various kinds of fruits— thus it is taught in the *Cintyaviśva*.
Therefore, one should cause the food offering (naivedya) to be presented first to the God of gods; then,
water for rinsing the mouth (gaṇḍūṣa) should be given with the hands joined in reverence.
One should discharge [the weapon] from the Astra-mantra once, three, or five times; then,
with the recitation of the nyāsa-mantras, one should fill each vessel with the radiant [liquid].
Above that, one should place the vessel and sprinkle it with water while reciting the heart-mantra.
Then, having performed the three *tāla*-claps, as well as the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) and the veiling (*avakuṇṭhana*),
one should display the *dhenu-mudrā* and then dismiss the eastern petal.

Food is of five kinds: that which is to be chewed, eaten, drunk, licked, and sucked. Having sprinkled the food with the Weapon-mantra, one should join it [to the mouth] using the tips of the middle finger, the ring finger, and the thumb, while reciting the Heart-mantra.
Having taken [the offering] from the hand of the Ācārya, one should present it into the hand of Gaurī;
and one should present the food offering (*naivedya*) into the hand of Śiva.
Just as the fruit of the wood-apple is consumed by an elephant,
so too should this essence of food be taken upon the tongue.
Having then discarded that flower, perform the washing of the hands;
one should offer it to Gaṇeśvara and the other deities by means of the *liṅga* alone.
Alternatively, one may present the cooked rice (*odana*) contained within a single vessel.
In the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"If there is no separate measurement for the limbs of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga*), it should be one [unit]. (L3) In the *Suprabheda*:
[With] one-fourth or one-eighth [of the size]...
(in the *Śivadharmottara*):
"He who should place [an offering] above Śiva, adorned with all red [colors],"
Listen now to the fruit of merit for one who offers a crown or ghee-water:
he shall dwell happily in the city of Śiva until the dissolution of all beings, traveling in celestial palaces (*vimāna*) by the millions, endowed with every object of desire.
Whoever should indeed place even a mere *tuṭi* of gold upon the head of the *liṅga*— [or a pearl, or a ruby]— for as long as this *siddhāsana* [remains], for that long fourteen Indras [shall endure].
Thus, one should understand the fruit to be equal according to one's wealth.
In the *Suprabheda*:
"On Sunday, a ruby; on Monday, a pearl;
on Tuesday, coral; and on Wednesday, there should be an emerald."
For Jupiter, there should be a topaz (*puṣyarāga*); for Venus, a diamond (*vajra*) is prescribed;
for Saturn, there should be a sapphire (*indranīla*), as well as all those [other gems] which [are traditionally mentioned].

On all days, the arrangement of ornaments is prescribed as appropriate; one should provide flowers and garments of those same colors. Regarding the portion for worship, one part shall be for the wrapping of garments.
The ornament for the wing [of the ritual vessel] should be adorned with two parts beautified by flowers;
one part should be filled with unbroken grains mixed with fragrant camphor,
and it is declared that the best incense is thoroughly saturated with honey.
Uśīra combined with sandalwood, mixed with honey and saturated with ghee—this is the characteristic of the lamp;
its portion is declared as before, and it is called the "middle" incense.
Guggulu mixed with clarified butter is declared to be the inferior incense;
guggulu mixed with clarified butter directly pleases Śaṅkara. Together with the counsel of the Dānavas, one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Camphor is offered as a lamp with cow-ghee and oil.
A lamp flame four, three, or two finger-breadths in length is distinguished;
for a lamp of tawny ghee, the cows should be black and red.
In the absence [of these], with goat-ghee or pure oil;
among these, ghee from a tawny cow (*kapilā*) is best, while ghee produced from other animals is middling.
Clarified butter from a goat and likewise pure oil are considered inferior;
they become Sāttvika, Rājasa, and Tāmasa respectively.
One should cause a lamp with camphor wicks to be offered, which bestows all perfections.
The lamp with a flame of four finger-breadths is the best; that with a flame of three finger-breadths is middling;
and that with a flame of two finger-breadths is declared to be the lowest. One should avoid using lamps made from the seeds of ordinary trees for the Śiva-lamp.
The incense burner has Agni as its presiding deity; the mouth is said to have Pāvaka as its deity;
the staff has Īśvara as its deity, and likewise the foot has Prajāpati.
The ninefold power and the new lamp [arise] from the wind of the seven islands;
in the five lamps are Nivṛtti and the others, and in the single lamp is Sarasvatī.
In the *Somaśambhu*, it is stated:

"Thereafter, one should offer water for sipping (ācamana) with the *Śiva-mantra* ending in *svadhā*, provided with *dūrvā* grass, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), *kuśa* grass, and accompanied by *bilva* leaves. (L4)
One should daily offer the *pavitraka* while reciting the root mantra,
[using grains] shaped like pearls or resembling pomegranate seeds. The wise person who worships with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) obtains imperishable fruit.
Since it is known through its falling, therefore this is indeed the purifier (*pavitraka*).
One should contemplate Śiva as being pleased by those beginning with Brahmā (*adhiriñca*) while they offer praise.
Next, I shall describe the *ārātrika*, which [removes] all defects...
The solar disc is indeed circular;
its central deity is Śrī, and Rātri is its presiding deity.
The best [offering] consists of nine lamps; the middling, five lamps;
and the inferior should consist of a single lamp, according to the sequence of the bowls.
As for the single lamp itself, one should sprinkle it with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*).
Then one should show the fragrant [incense] behind the lamp.
Having lifted it up, one should hold it and whirl it three times above the deity;
then, having whirled it three times from the feet up to the head, one should set it down.
O Ajita,
then, having taken ash scented with camphor and other fragrant substances,
and having grasped it with the [appropriate] mudrā, one should rub and swirl it three times over the liṅga.
One should then cast [the offering] into the lamp-vessel, and then upon the head of the *liṅga*;
thereafter, one should worship on the forehead with the root mantra (*mūla*) or else with the heart mantra (*hṛdaya*).
One should apply the *vṛtta* mark on the upward-facing [face], the *tripuṇḍra* on the eastern face,
the *triśūla* on the southern face, the square (*caturaśraka*) on the western face,
and the half-moon (*ardhacandra*) on the northern face; thus one should employ these [marks] for Śiva.
What is the purpose of protection for one whose eye is in the forehead?
(L3) One should cause the protection of the God to be bestowed above the eye on the forehead;
the Goddess, manifest in her true form, [should be placed] as a tilaka-mark on the front of the throat. (L4)
O Aṃśumatī, having performed the ritual touching of water, one should then show a mirror;
the mirror is Śiva-Śakti, and from that, the unborn Śiva shall arise. (L5)
The four circles are declared [to be] on the staff; it is called "the boy" in the *Śivadharmottara*.
One should offer a mirror made of clear [glass] to Śiva in front [of him].
For ten thousand times ten thousand eons, he is honored in the world of Śiva,
which is adorned with pearl necklaces as pure and stainless as the autumn moon.
One should give a parasol made of jewels or one made of gold;
adorned by that most variegated parasol being held [over him].
One shall dwell eternally in the City of Śiva, enjoying hundreds of celestial palaces.
In the *Tantrasāra*:
"And one should offer a vessel adorned with a jeweled handle to Śiva."
Or [he may give] a staff made of gold, silver, and so forth; hear now the fruit of his merit:
surrounded by celestial women with chowries held at the tips of their hands, possessing great enjoyments and dwelling in a celestial chariot, he shall reside for a long time in the city of Śiva.
Having fanned [it], Skanda was anointed with half [of it] for a year;
he is honored among the winds for thousands of millions of years. In the *Suprabheda*, in the *Suprabheda*.
Having given a peacock-feather fan to Śiva, it is exceedingly pleasing;
however, for the Sun, the fan is said to have a staff, a lotus, and a serpent.
The chowrie has the wind as its presiding deity; the handle is said to belong to Kārkoṭa.
On the Aṃśumatī [river], there is the parasol, the chowrie, the fan, and the palm-leaf whisk.
Having recollected the five Brahmans, one should indeed apply them in due order;
furthermore, one should cause [the disciple] to listen to the Purāṇas, the Āgamas, and the five ancillary sciences.
The invocation, the seat, the water for the feet, the respectful offering, the bath, the mouth-cleanser,
the sacred thread, the fragrance, the flower, the incense, the lamp, and the food offering.
Then, having offered water for sipping, drinking water, and betel leaf, and having performed a circumambulation,
one should worship Mahādeva with these sixteen types of service.
In the ritual procedure, the invitation and the seat are said there to consist of twelve measures;
the water for the feet consists of five measures, and likewise, the water for sipping consists of three measures.
The water for the guest-offering (*arghya*) should be one *mātrā*; the fragrance is said to be six *mātrās*.
The flower should be twelve *mātrās*, and the incense five. The lamp likewise should be six *mātrās*, while the collyrium for the eyes (*nīrāñjana*) is sixteen.
Afterwards, one should cause [the ashes] to be given; it is said that this consists of seven measures (*mātra*).
The fan should be three measures, while the fly-whisk (*śāmara*) should be ten.
The parasol (*chatra*) should be five measures, and the mirror (*darpaṇa*) should be one measure of a sage (*munimātra*).
Then one should present the food offering (naivedya), consisting of twenty-four items;
the water for the guest-offering (arghya) is for the pleasure of the gods, and the fragrance (gandha) is dear to Brahmā.
Flowers are known to bestow nourishment; incense is dear to Vaiśvānara;
the lamp is dear to the Sun; and the night-rite (ārātrika) should be known as bestowing victory.
It serves as protection for oneself and especially for the king;
the mirror bestows knowledge, and the parasol brings strength to the king.
The yak-tail whisk brings the destruction of enemies; song and instrumental music bring what is dear;
the sacrificial oblation brings prosperity in one's station; and water is the protector of life.
One should know that betel-leaf bestows prosperity, while the fire-oblation destroys disease.
If it is devoid of fragrance, there arises fear; if devoid of flowers, there is turmoil.
If devoid of incense, illness is certain; if devoid of a lamp, there is loss of intellect.
If the food offering (*naivedya*) is omitted, there will be famine; if the sacred fire is omitted, there will be turmoil.
For the domestic worship, one should fashion the sacrificial ladle (*sruc*), the large ladle (*sruva*), and other implements using the span of a finger.
In the case of the Preceptor (*ācārya*), the middle joint of the middle finger of the right hand [should serve as the measure].
And likewise, [the tree] Parvatāra; and I did not [measure it] by finger-breadths (*mātrāṅgula*).
[It was measured] by cubits (*paridhibhiḥ*) and by the span of a hand (*hastapramāṇataḥ*), as well as by its foliage (*palāśa*).
[This concerns] the worship of the tree in the temple of Koviḷa.

I shall describe the ritual for the worship of trees; listen attentively to that which destroys [misfortune] and increases longevity, prosperity, and fame, as well as the acquisition of sons and the increase of wealth.
Worship of trees is said to be twofold: general and specific.
The worship of trees such as the *aśvattha* and others is declared to be the general [form].
That particular tree among these which is inhabited by a deity through the presence of Śambhu is declared to be distinguished;
its worship has been described.
At the conclusion of the morning twilight,
however, the plastering should be thoroughly cleansed by means of a person in many forms, using the remnants from the tops of divine trees.
There, having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, and having sprinkled [the site] with water consecrated by the *astra-mantra*,
the Guru, having purified [the materials] such as the water for the feet (*pādya*) and worshipped them, should worship Vighneśa.
Then, having performed the worship of the door, the wise one should arrange the seat and the root-form of the Umā-tree named Hemin, as before.
Having meditated upon the tree as being composed of Śiva, one should perform the ritual bath as before;
one should offer clothing, garlands, and fragrant paste with the Śiva-mantra. Then, having offered the food offering (*naivedya*), one should present excellent incense and lamps.
The wise man should cause betel-leaf to be offered and should propitiate [the deity] with hymns and the like.
He should perform this once, twice, or thrice a day;
by performing worship day after day, he is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Thus ends the chapter on the ritual procedure for the worship of the Tree in the Kriyātantra of the Sūkṣmāgama.
[The Eightfold Hymn to the Nine Planets] May there be auspiciousness for Vighnarāja, the eternal Vināyaka, who is endowed with accomplishment and wisdom, for the pacification of all obstacles.

The radiant one, born of the Kāśyapa lineage, possessing the luster of the sun, the lord of the Leo zodiac, thirty-six years old, ten [fingers] in height, beautiful, Jupiter, Moon, and Mars— may he always be a good friend.
Venus is the enemy of Saturn; in Kaliṅga he is led [there], and Agnīśvara resides in Mevata.
In the center is a circle; in the eastern direction, the Sun shall always bring auspiciousness.
The Moon is the lord of Cancer, white in appearance, born of the Atri lineage.
The son of Candra (Mercury) is square-faced and belongs to Varuṇa; Umā is water, and Umā’s Lord (Śiva) is the Moon.

Having the auspicious fruits of six, seven, three, ten, and one [days], the enemy of Rāhu (Mercury), beloved of Budha and Arka, the lord born in the forest region, the maker of the cold rays—may he always grant prosperity.
Mars, the lord of the southern direction, resembles a triangle;
he is the sustainer and the lord of Scorpio and Aries. Jupiter is his friend, while Mercury is his enemy.
Mars bestows six, three, and one fruit respectively, and the Earth is his deity, as is Skanda.
May the son of the Earth, born of the Bhāradvāja lineage, always grant auspiciousness.
Saumya, Durmuṅmukha, Pītavarṇa, Makadhā, and he born of the Ātreya gotra;
Bāṇeśāna, Manasvahṛd, Ravīsuta, Śatrūṛdh, and another equal to them.
The maiden whose husband is [ruled by] ten, eight, four, six, five, three, or one [planets] brings auspiciousness;
may Mercury, whose presiding deity is Viṣṇu, always bestow prosperity.
[Mercury] belongs to the Aṅgiras gotra, faces north, and rules over the long Uttara[-nakṣatras].

Pīta, Aśva, Ardha, Śama, Sindhujanaka, Āpa, Yamīnādhipa, Sūrya, Indu, Kṣitija, Priya, Budha, Sita, Śatru, Sama, Sūrya, Saptākūdvibhava, and Suta—these [twelve] always bestow auspiciousness when they yield good results. (ll. 3–4)
Śukra, born of the Bhārgava lineage, is white in appearance; he faces the east, his direction being the eastern quarter.
He has five limbs, is the lord of Taurus and Libra, and his tree is the Udumbara.
Indrāṇī, Mukha, Śodhana, Śaśimitra, and Candrārava—
when the son of Bhṛgu (Venus) is devoid of six, eight, or ten [degrees] from these, he shall always bring auspiciousness.
Saturn is black in appearance, faces west, and belongs to the lineage of Kāśyapa.
Mercury and Venus are the lords of the hands and the water-pot; Mars and the Sun are the enemies.
The western direction is their station; the two gods Prajāpati and Yama are seated upon bows.
When situated in the sixth or third house, the son of the Sun (Saturn) shall always bring auspiciousness to the country. (8)
[The Eightfold Mantra] Haṃ haṃ haṃ! O you who laugh with your hand-nails, who hold a terrifying skull-bowl in your hand;
kṣaṃ kṣaṃ kṣaṃ! O Kālī, who bears a skeleton and holds a sword in your hand, you who are fashioned from the three worlds!

*Raṃ raṃ raṃ raṃga raṃgīrahasitavadane piṅgakeśī śmaśāne |* *Haṃ laṃ vaṃ sthāpanīye bhṛkuṭakuṭakuṭī bhopadaṃ khārakhajyam || 1 ||* *Hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ lambajihve kaha kaha kaha māṃ yehi yehi pracaṇḍī |* O you with a face laughing with passion, O tawny-haired one in the cremation ground! Haṃ laṃ vaṃ, you who are to be established, O frown-browed one, O you who are terrifying, O giver of fear, O you who are fierce! Hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ, O long-tongued one! Kaha kaha kaha! Come, come, O Pracaṇḍī!
Chuṃ chuṃ chuṃ! O wielder of the sword and the limbs! Kara kara kara! (*). O Hṛjjvālinī, Piṅgalākṣī! (*).

He bhe bhe, O you who pierce! Bilu bilu, O you who laugh! Caṇḍike, O you of fierce form! Hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ māṃ klīṃ! O Bakṣe, O you who are completely dissolved at the end of the aeon! O you whose form is naked, whose nature is the essential sound! 2.
O you who are terrible with your immediate accoutrements, *lalalalalalitā*, holding a trident in hand, praised one; O *raudrī*, *kūśmāṇḍī*, *ha ha ha ha*, *bhairavī*, *ugrakeśī*!
*Hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ phaṭ*! O *karālī*, together with my guru, O *sukeśī*, mistress of the *preta*s!
Who, who has commanded with hands raised? Protect me, O Bhadrakālī! || 3 ||

The yoginī is Hana Hana Hana Kṛṣṇa Kṛṣṇasvarūpī; she eternally blazes with tridents, Dhaga Dhaga Dhagatī, the protectress of all, Caṇḍī. Hrāṃ Hrīṃ Hrūṃ Kālī Kālī, the sharp night-stalker, Vajracaṇḍī, Pracaṇḍī.
A certain skull-bearer, with a deformed human head upon his crown and a garland of skulls [around his waist], || 4 ||
In the sky, she is indeed Tālaka; at the end of the dissolution, she is the naked one, her own true nature.

Between wood and stone, in the abode of fire, she is Raudradaṇḍī, the Mistress of the Gaṇas. With hanging lips, she is in the intermediate space; throughout the quarters and the days, she is the eternally moving Kālī.
O Cakrī, dwelling in the netherworld (pātāla), the cause of the three worlds—protect me, O Bhadrakālī!

(5) KHRĀṂ KHRĪṂ KHRŪṂ! You who possess a single form, the burner of the world-ocean, whose sound is like a thunderclap, O Goddess of the wind-region, with a most beautiful radiance, you who dwell in eternal union with the one Yoga!

Maṃ maṃ maṃ! O Māthi, Māthi, you who are the embodiment of the mantra, the supreme deity of the Kuḍakulakula lineage, Durgī, by virtue of your vast and noble family that grants liberation from Durga, O dark-complexioned one, salutations to you! 6.
Bhā bhā bhā, O you who exist through the manifestation of all things! Be, be, bestower of worldly enjoyment and liberation together with existence!
Phī phī phī phī-karambi! Guha, Guha, O you who are the leader of the Guhas! O you who possess excellent enjoyments, excellent enjoyments!
Bhu bhu bhu! O you who cause the trembling of the earth! O you whose qualities are as vast as the sky and its hosts! Homage to you, the one with a sword in hand! Homage to you!
Phe phe phe, O you who pierce! Hara hara hara me, phaṭ! Karālī, homage to you! || 7 || O fierce one, of fierce nature, you who are abundant in gentleness, the truth-bestowing Mataṅgī;
you whose form is terrible as Time, whose face is yellowed by human [flesh], the virtuous goddess of the virtuous! || 8 ||

*klīṃ buṃ lūṃ*, O Goddess who wears bracelets made of the serpent-king and the lion, who resides in the row of Brahmā, O Mahendrī, *oṃ oṃ oṃ*, O Śāntadevī accompanied by the *kṣipralamba* and the *ḍamaruka* drum, salutations to you! 8.
[The eight mantras are complete. Rāhu is born from Siṃhaladeśa; Niṛti is [born from] Akhaṇḍin. The *tantukramuka* is Apṛkṣā; Kālī is the *parṇaka*.
If the powder is not purified by these three, heaven does not exist.

May the Goddess who is the Fortune of the lineage, the Fortune of the forest-king, the daughter of the Milky Ocean, whose eyes are as long as lotuses, the consort of Śrī Viṣṇu, the sole mother of the world—may she grant boons to the bride and groom. (v.
3) Having clothed [her]... the daughter of the mountain king, with divine golden garments and jewel ornaments...
May Kalyāṇagaurī, along with the auspicious bride and groom, be bestowers of boons.
"Hail! May the mantras and their meanings be true and fruitful, O venerable ones! May you great ones show favor toward this god, the Great God."
